text: When Johnson came to write his Preface, the question he set himself was why Shakespeare should still be read and acted when most of the dramatists who shared his stage had fallen out of notice. His answer is plain, and he gives it early: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature." (Johnson 1765). Those dramatists drew men as they found them in the London of their own day; they caught the fashions and follies peculiar to a single street or a single decade, and when those passed, the figures built upon them passed too. Shakespeare, in Johnson's account, looked beneath such accidents to the passions and motives which any age will recognise. His persons act from love, ambition, jealousy and grief as these are felt everywhere. The particular habit of Elizabethan England sits lightly upon them. A reader who knows nothing of that habit can still find Lear's rage or Falstaff's evasions true to what he has seen of men. Johnson took the long survival of Shakespeare's audience as the proof of it.
